title: Peace returns
hookLine: Punjab grew quieter, and families began to heal

cards: A shopkeeper in a Punjab town pulls his shutter down long after dark, for the first time in years. Nobody knocks. Nothing happens.
He walks home. That's what peace looked like in Punjab when it came back: not a parade, but small, ordinary things done again without fear. A farmer turning water onto his field at night.
A wedding with music until late. Buses running on time. Slowly, the fighting faded, and Punjab grew quieter.

teach.b: First, the quiet. The armed groups were broken up or faded away, elections were held again, and ordinary life came back to towns and villages.
Historians argue about how it happened and at what cost, and about how much of it came from police force. Less disputed is that daily life changed. Second, what the quiet didn't fix.
Mothers were still waiting for sons who had disappeared. Widows in Delhi were still going to court. Families on every side had empty chairs at the table.

teach.h: PEACE DID NOT CLOSE OLD WOUNDS.
teach.b: Peace stopped new wounds. It did not close the old ones. Third, the medicine.

In Asa di Var, at Ang 469, Guru Nanak says something strange: suffering became the medicine, and comfort the disease. Pain, in that line, can push a person back toward the Lord, where easy days let them forget.
Some Sikh families who lived through these years turned to gurbani, to sangat and to seva, not to erase what happened, but to carry it. Fourth, a look back.

teach.h: A WEEK FROM FIELDS TO QUIET.
teach.b: This week began in Punjab's green fields.
Then came the Anandpur resolution, read two ways; a Vaisakhi clash in Amritsar; June, remembered as the third ghallughara; the widows' colony in Delhi; and Khalra counting the missing.
It ends here, with quiet, and the slow work after it.
Healing is not forgetting. It is learning to live beside the empty chair.

how: Sikh families who lost loved ones in these years remember them in Ardas and in gurdwara programs, and some still seek records and justice while getting on with daily life.

games.why: Punjab's families got on with daily life while still remembering their dead and, for some, still asking for justice. healing, slowly.

practice: Bring to mind one wound that hasn't closed, your own, a family's or a place's, and don't try to fix it.

Let each breath out be a little longer than the breath in; healing doesn't happen in two minutes, and it doesn't need to, because you're just sitting beside it. If you pray, pray for healing in your own words, or rest on Waheguru.
